summary: Specifies the Accumulated IGP Metric attribute for BGP, so that within a single administration with several contiguous BGP networks, BGP can choose paths based on a summed metric, as an IGP would.

eli5.summary: BGP normally does not add up distances. When one company runs many linked networks, it can add up distances along the way and choose the shortest.

questions: how does bgp use igp metric
when is the aigp attribute sent between ases
subtitle: A BGP attribute that carries an accumulated IGP-style distance, so BGP can pick the shortest path inside one administration.

tldr.problem: BGP does not choose paths by a metric, but some administrations run several contiguous BGP networks and want IGP-like shortest-path routing across them.
tldr.mechanism: The optional, non-transitive AIGP attribute (type code 26) holds a 64-bit accumulated metric that routers add to when they change the next hop, and the BGP decision process compares it before its usual tie-breakers.
tldr.outcome: Within one AIGP administrative domain BGP can choose the lowest-distance path, while strict rules keep the attribute from leaking onto the wider Internet.

today: RFC 7311 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why BGP Has No Metric, and Why Add One
sections.content:
Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) give each link a metric and choose the path whose summed distance is smallest. BGP was built for many administrative domains with little coordination, and it does not choose by a metric. The RFC gives two reasons: local distance changes would be propagated around the Internet, violating the principle that changes of only local significance must not have global effects, and domains need not reveal or agree on policies.

Some deployments are different: one administration runs a network split into several contiguous ASes, for example because an IGP does not scale well there. In that case BGP can usefully follow the IGP metric. Using the MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) attribute for this is not enough, since the decision process gives priority to other factors such as AS_PATH length, and the MED procedures do not accumulate the metric along the path.

RFC 7311 therefore defines a new optional, non-transitive attribute, the Accumulated IGP Metric or AIGP attribute. It must not leak out of the AIGP administrative domain, and it must be accumulated along the whole path, so it does not appear where the IGP metric is unknown.
sections.eli5: Most of the internet does not measure distance in one shared way, because every network has its own rules. But inside one company, adding up the distances is useful, so this RFC adds a way to do that.

sections.title: The AIGP Attribute Format
sections.content:
The AIGP attribute is an optional, non-transitive BGP path attribute with type code 26. Its value is a set of Type/Length/Value elements. The Type is one octet, the Length is two octets and counts the whole TLV including Type and Length (so the minimum is 3), and the Value holds zero or more octets.

Only one TLV is defined, the AIGP TLV: Type 1, Length 11, and an 8-octet Value read as an unsigned 64-bit integer. The wide field means it can hold the sum of an arbitrary number of 4-octet IGP metrics. An attribute SHOULD contain no more than one AIGP TLV; if there are several, only the first is used and the others MUST be passed along unchanged.

Malformed attributes

A malformed AIGP attribute is treated exactly like an unrecognized non-transitive attribute: quietly ignored and not passed on. An attribute with the transitive bit set is malformed. A first TLV holding the maximum value 0xffffffffffffffff SHOULD be treated as malformed too, since it cannot grow any further. Several TLVs of one type, or TLVs of unknown types, do not make it malformed.
sections.eli5: The attribute is a small note stuck to a route. The note has a label, a length, and one big number that says how far away the destination is so far.

sections.title: Where It Is Sent, Created and Updated
sections.content:
An implementation MUST have a per-session setting AIGP_SESSION. It SHOULD default to enabled for IBGP sessions and for EBGP sessions between members of the same BGP Confederation, and MUST default to disabled for all other EBGP sessions. The attribute MUST NOT be sent on a session where it is disabled. If one is received there, it is ignored, but the event SHOULD be logged in a rate-limited manner.

Creating the attribute is controlled by AIGP_ORIGINATE, whose default MUST be disabled. A speaker MUST NOT add the attribute to a route whose path leads outside its AIGP administrative domain, and only to static routes, IGP routes redistributed into BGP, IBGP-learned routes with an empty AS_PATH, or EBGP-learned routes whose AS_PATH holds only ASes of the same domain. It MUST NOT add it to a route for which it has not set itself as next hop. The initial value follows policy, for example the IGP-computed distance from the originator to the prefix.

When a router passes a route on and changes the next hop, it MUST add the distance to the old next hop to the value, by a non-zero amount, and the value MUST be capped at its maximum and never wrap around. If the next hop is not changed, the value MUST NOT change. If the route to the old next hop itself needs recursive resolution, the RFC gives a step-by-step procedure that adds the AIGP values found along the recursion.
sections.eli5: Each router that takes over a route adds the distance to the previous stop onto the note. The note is only passed around inside one company, and it cannot be allowed to leave the building.

sections.title: Changes to Path Selection
sections.content:
The AIGP rules plug into the tie-breaking part of the BGP decision process of RFC 4271. If only one route has the highest degree of preference, or a route is already eliminated (for example by an AS-PATH loop or an unresolvable next hop), AIGP is not considered.

When tie-breaking runs, the AIGP step MUST come before the existing tie-breakers. If any route has an AIGP attribute with an AIGP TLV, routes without one are removed. For each remaining route, the router computes A as the route's AIGP TLV value plus the IGP distance from itself to the route's next hop, and keeps only the routes tied for the lowest A.

The RFC also replaces the "interior cost" tie-breaker with an "AIGP-enhanced interior cost": the AIGP value of the installed route to the next hop (0 if it has none) plus the IGP distance to the final resolved next hop.
sections.eli5: When a router has several ways to get somewhere, it adds up the distance notes plus its own distance to the first stop, and picks the smallest total.

sections.title: Deployment Cautions
sections.content:
The RFC only considers networks where every router tunnels packets to its BGP next hop. Using the attribute elsewhere is out of scope. Mixing different IGPs (such as OSPF and IS-IS), or IGPs whose metrics mean different things such as bandwidth and latency, is unlikely to give sensible results, as is an inter-AS link metric that is not comparable to the IGP metrics.

  • The procedures work best with multiple paths available, so the RFC highly recommends using them together with best-external advertisement and ADD-PATH.
  • A Route Reflector that does not pass all paths tends to pass those with the smallest IGP distance to the next hop, which may be non-optimal for clients. A reflector that supports AIGP when some clients do not can also produce unintended routing.
  • Frequent IGP distance changes can cause equally frequent BGP updates. The originator MAY suppress an update when the change is below a configurable threshold.
  • "Costing out" a link raises the AIGP value as it would raise the IGP distance, but a route carrying AIGP is always preferred over one without it, whatever the value.
sections.eli5: This works well only if every part of the network measures distance the same way. Mix miles and minutes, and the totals make no sense.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC lists two risks. A spurious AIGP attribute, introduced by error or malfeasance, could cause selection of paths other than those desired. Misconfiguration on both ends of an EBGP connection could pass the attribute from one service provider to another, which would likely lead to an unsound selection of paths.

IANA assigned codepoint 26 in the BGP Path Attributes registry and created the "BGP AIGP Attribute Types" registry. Its Type field is one octet with values 1 to 255, 0 is Reserved, registration needs Standards Action, and Type 1 is AIGP.
sections.eli5: If a wrong note sneaks in, routers could pick a bad road. So the rule is to keep the notes inside, and to double check both sides when two companies connect.
